identification: Single-sided vitreous enamel advertising strip sign, white sans-serif letters on cobalt blue: 'LEADING NEWSPAPER. / THE DAILY TELEGRAPH. / TASMANIA.' with 'MADE IN ENGLAND' small at lower right. 15 x 53 cm (catalogue). The Daily Telegraph was the Launceston daily paper (1883 to 1928, when it merged into The Examiner), so the sign predates 1928, probably 1900s to 1920s. Condition: top right corner has a large chunk missing or torn away with rust along the broken edge (the plate outline steps down there, so this is metal loss, not just chipping); small chips and rust at the fixing holes along top and bottom edges and at the corners; face enamel otherwise bright with good gloss and little fading. Back (photo 4) is rusted with green/grey counter-enamel and white enamel drips, consistent with genuine period enamel, not a modern reproduction (reproductions are usually printed tin or have clean backs).
marks_seen: 'MADE IN ENGLAND' lower right on the face. No enameller name visible in the photos (could be on the lower edge or back but nothing legible).
google_searches: Google: '"Daily Telegraph" Tasmania enamel sign "leading newspaper"' (Trove ads 1910 and 1911 confirm 'TASMANIA'S LEADING NEWSPAPER, THE DAILY TELEGRAPH, LAUNCESTON' was the paper's slogan); Google Lens on photo 1 (found a modern made-to-order reproduction on eBay and the Roycroft 2018 lot); '"daily telegraph" tasmania enamel sign sold'; '"Daily Telegraph" Launceston enamel sign'; '"telegraph" "tasmania" enamel sign auction lot blue'. antiquesigns.com.au blog lists a 'The Daily Telegraph Tasmania' sign made by Laughtons Enamelling, Footscray, so at least two versions exist (Australian-made Laughtons and this English-made one).

resale_estimate: A$150-280 to a Tasmanian collector; realistic A$200. On mainland eBay probably A$120-180. The missing top right corner is the big drag; a clean example might make A$300-400.
doubts: Only one recorded same-sign appearance (Roycroft 2018, estimate A$80-100 for a fair one, result not found), so this is thin. The bidding (11 bids, A$220 with 59487 and 122213 trading bids) is Tasmanian collectors chasing a Launceston paper's sign, which is a genuine local premium, not hidden value. It looks genuine: square corners with fixing holes, 'MADE IN ENGLAND', period full stops, rusted back with counter-enamel drips. Reproductions exist (eBay seller makes them) but differ visibly. Current A$220 plus 22% premium = A$268, already at or over what I could confidently resell it for.
viewing_check: Check the broken corner: is the metal torn off (loss) or bent back? Look along the bottom and back edges for an enameller's name (Wildman, Patent Enamel, Chromo, Falkirk, Bruton). Check the back is heavy steel with counter-enamel (genuine) rather than thin tin. Note chip count around the holes.

identification: Single-sided flat green sign with cream/yellow serif capitals 'BP / AUSTRALIA / LTD.' and a much smaller, heavily worn white line at the bottom that reads as 'INCORPORATED IN VICTORIA'. 54 x 39 cm (catalogue; looks squarish in photos), rounded corners, four fixing holes. This is a company name plate for a BP Australia Ltd office, depot or terminal, not a forecourt brand sign (no shield logo). BP Australia Ltd took that name in 1957 (formerly Commonwealth Oil Refineries) and was incorporated in Victoria, so the sign is 1957 or later, probably 1957 to 1970s. Condition: face is clean with good colour; small chip/rust at top left hole and a few specks; the bottom 'Incorporated in Victoria' line is almost entirely worn away; back (photo 4) is black with rust spotting.
marks_seen: 'INCORPORATED IN VICTORIA' (worn) along the bottom. No enameller's mark visible.

identification: Keen's Genuine Tasmanian Curry Powder 4 oz canister, cylindrical tin (grey metal push-on lid and base rim) wrapped in a dark blue paper label printed in gold: 'Keen's Genuine Tasmanian Curry Powder, manufactured at Kingston, Browns River', central roundel of the 1866-7 Intercolonial Exhibition (Melbourne) medal 'Medal awarded to J Keen', jurors' report text, 'Manufactured by Keen's Curry Powder Co.', '4 OZS. Condition: label scuffed with a tear/lift along the top edge and corner, rust on the base rim, contents unknown.

identification: Three handmade soft red clay bricks (not 'items' of metal: the catalogue lot is '3 BROAD ARROW STAMPED CONVICT BRICKS - EX-ALANVALE NEWNHAM', i.e. bricks recovered from Alanvale, Newnham, Launceston). Each has marks hand-incised into the wet clay before firing (drawn with a finger or stick, not a stamped frog): brick 1 (larger, paler, mortar on one edge) reads roughly 'L ^ D' with a broad arrow between letters; brick 2 has a single vertical stroke beside a large broad arrow; brick 3 reads roughly 'W ^ W' (or W ^ M) with a broad arrow in the middle. Bricks 2 and 3 also show deep finger/thumb impressions at the corners, the classic sign of hand moulding seen on Tasmanian convict-made bricks. These are consistent with genuine colonial (convict-era, c.1820s-1850s) Van Diemen's Land government bricks: broad arrow plus moulder's/gang initials scratched by hand is the typical Tasmanian convict pattern; later government issue used stamped marks in a frog, not hand scratching. Provenance (Alanvale) cannot be verified from photos. Bulky-ish and heavy (3 bricks, perhaps 9-10 kg).
marks_seen: Brick 1: incised 'L', broad arrow, 'D' (approx). Brick 2: incised vertical stroke and broad arrow. Brick 3: incised 'W', broad arrow, 'W'. Finger/thumb impressions on bricks 2 and 3. No frog, no impressed maker's stamp visible.

resale_estimate: A$250-450 for the three if sold one at a time (A$80-150 each realistic, A$200+ for the best one with clear initials and arrow on a good auction day). As a single lot at a general auction, about A$150-250.
doubts: Broad arrows on bricks are faked by scratching old bricks after firing; these look incised wet (soft-edged grooves, same fired colour inside the groove, finger marks), but that needs checking in hand. 'Ex-Alanvale Newnham' provenance is the vendor's and unverified; I found no recorded convict establishment at Alanvale (the bricks could have been reused in a later building there). The NSW bidder leading suggests a convict-brick collector is already in. Weight/postage: about 3 kg each, so eBay resale costs A$20-30 postage per brick, which eats margin.
viewing_check: Look closely at the grooves: wet-incised marks have smooth rounded edges, slightly raised clay burr at the sides and the same fired skin inside the groove; a fresh scratch on a fired brick shows sharper edges, paler or brighter clay inside and cuts through the fire skin. Check for old lime mortar (supports building origin). Note sizes (Tasmanian convict bricks commonly about 225-240 mm). Check for chips/spalls on the marked faces.

identification: Cardboard tray of garage/automobilia bits. Every piece, from the two photos: (1) RAC car badge: cast, nickel/chrome finish, crowned oval with rope/laurel border and large interlaced 'RAC' monogram, no enamel, mounting bolt on the back; early style (likely pre-war to 1950s), possibly an Australian RAC club badge rather than the UK enamel Union Jack type; the best piece. (2) Bedford round cast alloy badge with the Vauxhall griffin and 'BEDFORD' in a diagonal band, worn plating; looks like a Bedford truck hubcap or horn-push centre badge, 1950s-60s. (3) 'WAYFARER Road Liner' stamped aluminium plate with an Indian-head/arrow logo and star field, about 40 cm, from an Australian Wayfarer caravan (Wayfarer also made Landliner motorhomes in the 1970s). (4) Ford blue oval badge, enamel/plastic insert, 1970s-90s. (5) Ford blue oval mounted in a teal metallic plastic surround: a Ford bonnet/grille ornament from a 1970s-80s Falcon/Cortina era car (exact model unconfirmed). (6) Toyota chrome emblem, modern (1990s+). (7) Copper/brass-coloured pump oiler with long spout (no maker visible). (8) Blue hand pump oiler and (9) red hand pump oiler, matching the Australian REGA pump oiler pattern. (10) Green pressed-steel thumb-trigger oiler with long spout and grip ring. (11) Two pressed-steel push-bottom oil cans with spiral flexible spouts, rusty (one has a small paper label on the spout). (12) 'CARBOX' printed tin box (yellow border, landscape/pyramid scene), lid missing, with a black tin inside; Carbox was a 1920s petrol bowser brand (NZ/AU), so this may be a related garage tin; label too blurred to confirm. (13) Two galvanised pipe fittings/couplings (scrap). No Shell, Castrol or brass-bodied oilers of real value seen.

identification: Cast iron wall-mounted yoke bell (farm / dinner / school style), approx 30 cm mouth diameter, 50 cm overall height. Wall plate with 4 bolt holes, U-shaped hanging bracket, pivoting yoke with acorn finial, swinging pull arm for a rope, iron clapper tied with twine. Black painted finish, light rust at pivots. Pattern matches the common US farm-bell format (C.S. Bell / Hillsboro style) and the many later reproductions. Catalogue: estimate A$150-250; current bid A$220 at 10 Nov. Google Lens on photo 1: closest matches are modern 'antique style' cast iron school/dinner bells, eg The Renmy Store 'Large Cast Iron School Dinner Bell' 51 cm H x 38 cm W, 8.7 kg, A$239.95 new (same wall plate, U bracket, yoke, acorn finial and rope arm, though the lot's plate has 4 holes and a chamfered top). The clean casting, absence of any foundry name or 'No.' size mark and the twine-tied clapper point to a 20th/21st century reproduction rather than a 19th century C.S. Bell, Crystal Metal or similar US foundry bell (those carry cast names, size numbers and 1886 patent dates on the yoke). Estimated weight 8-12 kg.
marks_seen: None visible in 4 photos (no foundry name, size number or date on yoke, bell shoulder or bracket). Paper lot tag only.

doubts: Verdict supports: A$400 hammer (A$488 with 22% BP) leaves room against a realistic A$450-700 resale, though the margin is modest once selling costs and time are counted. Only one same-model sale has a visible price (A$750, 33 bids, no reserve, Nov 2023). Two more same-model sales in 2026 (AuctionsPlus Walcha and Wellington) are confirmed SOLD but the prices sit behind a login, which I did not use. The Oct 2026 MRE lot (Thumpa plus a petrol compressor for a A$600 top bid) points to softer money now, which is why I would not chase it past A$400.
